# What I compare with Homework 4

I use **1970 only**, the same year as the revised Homework 4. I keep its
log-rainfall model, elevation trend and spherical residual covariance.
The new question is how the estimates and prediction intervals change
when I account for parameter uncertainty with Bayesian kriging.

Likelihood kriging uses fitted covariance parameters. Bayesian kriging
allows them to vary according to their posterior distribution. I compare
the two methods on the same data, grid and five validation folds, refitting
both within each training set. Both predict a new observation, including
the nugget. I keep the model structure chosen in Homework 4, so this
comparison does not test the earlier model-selection step independently.

## Data and the prediction target

```{r data}
data_env <- new.env()
invisible(load("data/RainData.RData", envir = data_env))
dat <- subset(data_env$dati, anno == 1970)
grid <- data_env$grid
region_fix <- c("4085" = "Basilicata", "4086" = "Basilicata",
                "4367" = "Calabria")
dat$Nome_Regione <- as.character(dat$Nome_Regione)
i <- dat$ID %in% as.numeric(names(region_fix))
dat$Nome_Regione[i] <- unname(region_fix[as.character(dat$ID[i])])
stopifnot(nrow(dat) == 189, all(dat$anno == 1970), !anyNA(dat),
  !anyNA(grid), all(dat$totanno > 0), !anyDuplicated(dat$ID),
  !anyDuplicated(dat[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]),
  !anyDuplicated(grid[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]))
prepare <- function(d) {
  d$x <- d$XUTM/1000
  d$y <- d$YUTM/1000
  d$elev <- d$Quota/1000
  d
}
dat <- prepare(dat)
grid <- prepare(grid)
dat$rain <- dat$totanno
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(~elev, dat))$rank == 2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Year = 1970, Stations = nrow(dat),
  Grid_points = nrow(grid), Mean_rainfall = mean(dat$rain),
  Cor_rain_elevation = cor(dat$rain, dat$Quota)), digits = 2)
```

All 189 stations remain in the analysis, including the three corrected
regional labels. The matching land grid is inside `RainData.RData`.
As in Homework 4, I interpret rainfall as mm, elevation as m, and the
supplied projected coordinates as m before converting distances to km.
Those units are assumptions based on the supplied names and values;
the file does not provide full coordinate-system metadata.

The target is **annual rainfall at an unobserved station-like location**.
It includes the nugget variation. I explicitly set `signal = FALSE` for
both prediction methods, because their default settings differ in `geoR`.

# The Bayesian model and priors

I use the same observation model as Homework 4:
\[
\log Y(s)=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{elevation}(s)/1000+w(s)+\epsilon(s).
\]
The spatial residual $w(s)$ has partial sill $\sigma^2$ and spherical
range $\phi$. The independent nugget has variance $\tau^2$.
The spherical correlation reaches zero at distance $\phi$. Stationarity
and isotropy refer to the residual process after accounting for elevation.
The Gaussian approximation is on the log scale, not the rainfall scale.

I use `geoR::krige.bayes`. It works over a grid of range and relative-nugget
values and draws from the resulting posterior. This is direct simulation,
not MCMC. I check simulation noise, grid resolution and prior sensitivity.

## My prior choices

I define $\eta=\tau^2/\sigma^2$. This is a ratio to the **partial sill**,
not the nugget fraction of total variance; that fraction is $\eta/(1+\eta)$.

| Quantity | Prior used |
|:--|:--|
| Trend coefficients | Flat prior: $p(\beta_0,\beta_1)\propto 1$ |
| Partial sill | $\sigma^2=4(0.1)/U$, with $U\sim\chi^2_4$ |
| Range $\phi$ | Values 10, 30, ..., 610 km, with weights proportional to $\exp(-\phi/150)$ |
| Relative nugget $\eta$ | Equal probabilities on 0, 0.05, ..., 1.50 |

The flat trend prior does not favour a particular intercept or elevation
effect. It is an improper prior, but gives a proper posterior here because
the trend matrix has full rank and the remaining priors are proper.
The partial-sill prior is a scaled inverse-chi-squared prior.
The range prior favours shorter ranges but has a long tail. I examine what
this means for rainfall dependence in Section 5. These are modelling choices,
not uniquely correct priors. I keep them fixed across validation folds and
do not use held-out rainfall to set their values.

```{r bayesian-functions}
make_g <- function(d) {
  geoR::as.geodata(data.frame(x = d$x, y = d$y,
    z = log(d$rain), elev = d$elev), covar.col = 4)
}

make_prior <- function(step = 20, range_scale = 150) {
  geoR::prior.control(beta.prior = "flat",
    sigmasq.prior = "sc.inv.chisq",
    sigmasq = 0.1, df.sigmasq = 4,
    phi.prior = "exponential", phi = range_scale,
    phi.discrete = seq(10, 610, by = step),
    tausq.rel.prior = "uniform",
    tausq.rel.discrete = seq(0, 1.5, by = step/400))
}

bayes_fit <- function(d, locations = NULL, seed = 5001,
                      prior = make_prior(), draws = 20000) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X <- geoR::trend.spatial(~elev, d)
  if (is.null(locations)) {
    b <- geoR::krige.bayes(make_g(d),
      model = geoR::model.control(trend.d = X,
        cov.model = "spherical", lambda = 1), prior = prior,
      output = geoR::output.control(n.posterior = draws, messages = FALSE))
  } else {
    b <- geoR::krige.bayes(make_g(d),
      locations = as.matrix(locations[c("x", "y")]),
      model = geoR::model.control(trend.d = X,
        trend.l = geoR::trend.spatial(~elev, locations),
        cov.model = "spherical", lambda = 1), prior = prior,
      output = geoR::output.control(n.posterior = draws,
        n.predictive = draws, simulations.predictive = TRUE,
        quantile = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), mean.var = FALSE,
        moments = FALSE, signal = FALSE, messages = FALSE))
  }
  list(posterior = b$posterior, predictive = b$predictive)
}

bayes_summary <- function(b, columns = NULL) {
  sim <- b$predictive$simulations
  if (!is.null(columns)) sim <- sim[, columns, drop = FALSE]
  q <- exp(t(apply(sim, 1, quantile,
                  probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)))
  data.frame(Lower = q[, 1], Median = q[, 2], Upper = q[, 3])
}

boundary <- function(b) {
  p <- b$posterior
  c(phi_low = unname(head(p$phi$distribution, 1)),
    phi_high = unname(tail(p$phi$distribution, 1)),
    eta_low = unname(head(p$tausq.rel$distribution, 1)),
    eta_high = unname(tail(p$tausq.rel$distribution, 1)))
}
```

I log rainfall explicitly and use `lambda = 1` inside `geoR`, so it is not
transformed twice. Exponentiating the log-scale predictive quantiles gives
the corresponding rainfall-scale quantiles.

## Credible intervals and posterior predictive intervals

A **95% credible interval** gives uncertainty about a parameter, such as
the elevation coefficient or range, given the data and model.

A **95% posterior predictive interval** concerns rainfall at a new location.
It includes parameter uncertainty, spatial variation and the nugget. These
are the intervals on the Bayesian maps. Homework 4 instead uses approximate
likelihood-based prediction intervals.

I use central equal-tailed intervals, with 2.5% in each tail. They are not
HPD intervals. The predictive intervals are pointwise; they do not provide
simultaneous 95% coverage for the entire map.

## Why I compare predictive medians

I use the **predictive median** as the point prediction for both methods.
It is the value with half the predictive probability below it and half
above it. I assess it with MAE, which is appropriate for a median forecast.

There is a mathematical reason for this choice. The conjugate variance
prior gives a mixture of Student-t predictive distributions on the log
scale. After exponentiation, this model has no finite arithmetic rainfall
mean, even though its central quantiles are well defined. I therefore do
not average simulated rainfall values or report a Bayesian rainfall mean.
This is a limitation of the model's extreme tails, and a reason to focus
on quantiles. The Interval Score below evaluates those interval endpoints
against the observed held-out rainfall.

Homework 4 mapped likelihood predictive **means**. For the side-by-side
maps here, I also calculate likelihood **medians**. Its interval formula
and its original mean-based RMSE are retained for reference. This keeps
the two point maps comparable and makes the change of summary explicit.

# A fair predictive comparison

## Refit the Homework 4 model

```{r likelihood-functions}
fit_ml <- function(d) {
  g <- make_g(d)
  s2 <- mean(resid(lm(log(rain) ~ elev, data = d))^2)
  fits <- lapply(c(20, 80), function(start) {
    tryCatch(geoR::likfit(g, trend = ~elev, cov.model = "spherical",
      ini.cov.pars = c(0.8*s2, start), nugget = 0.2*s2,
      fix.nugget = FALSE, lambda = 1, fix.lambda = TRUE,
      lik.method = "ML", limits = geoR::pars.limits(phi = c(0.5, 1500)),
      messages = FALSE, control = list(maxit = 2000)),
      error = function(e) NULL)
  })
  ok <- vapply(fits, function(f) {
    !is.null(f) && is.finite(f$loglik) &&
      f$info.minimisation.function$convergence == 0
  }, logical(1))
  if (!any(ok)) stop("No converged maximum-likelihood fit.")
  fits <- fits[ok]
  fits[[which.max(vapply(fits, function(f) f$loglik, numeric(1)))]]
}

predict_ml <- function(d, locations, fit) {
  p <- geoR::krige.conv(make_g(d),
    locations = as.matrix(locations[c("x", "y")]),
    krige = geoR::krige.control(type.krige = "OK", obj.model = fit,
      trend.d = geoR::trend.spatial(~elev, d),
      trend.l = geoR::trend.spatial(~elev, locations), micro.scale = 0),
    output = geoR::output.control(signal = FALSE, messages = FALSE))
  data.frame(Lower = exp(p$predict-qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(p$krige.var)),
    Median = exp(p$predict),
    Upper = exp(p$predict+qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(p$krige.var)),
    Mean = exp(p$predict+p$krige.var/2))
}

scores <- function(y, p) {
  interval_score <- p$Upper-p$Lower +
    40*pmax(p$Lower-y, 0) + 40*pmax(y-p$Upper, 0)
  c(IS95 = mean(interval_score), MAE = mean(abs(p$Median-y)),
    Coverage = 100*mean(y >= p$Lower & y <= p$Upper),
    Width = mean(p$Upper-p$Lower))
}
```

## Proper scores and validation design

The main comparison uses the **95% Interval Score**:
\[
IS_{0.05}(l,u;y)=(u-l)+40(l-y)1(y<l)+40(y-u)1(y>u).
\]
It rewards useful narrow intervals and penalises missed observations.
It is a proper score for central interval forecasts under the usual
finite-loss conditions: the true 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles minimise its
expected value. Lower is better. I also report MAE for the median,
coverage and average interval width. All reported scores are in mm,
except coverage, which is a percentage.

I use the exact Homework 4 split: five folds and seed `2026 + 1970`.
Every training fold refits both methods. Bayesian predictions use the
posterior from that training fold, not the full-data posterior. I use
20,000 posterior predictive draws per fold and keep the priors fixed.

```{r cache-key, include=FALSE}
analysis_key <- list(tools::md5sum("data/RainData.RData"),
  lapply(list(prepare, make_g, make_prior, bayes_fit, bayes_summary,
              boundary, fit_ml, predict_ml, scores), deparse),
  as.character(packageVersion("geoR")))
```

```{r validation, cache=TRUE, cache.vars=c("fold","ml_cv","bayes_cv","cv_half1","cv_half2","boundary_cv"), cache.extra=analysis_key}
set.seed(2026 + 1970)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(dat)))
ml_cv <- data.frame(Lower = rep(NA_real_, nrow(dat)),
                    Median = NA_real_, Upper = NA_real_, Mean = NA_real_)
bayes_cv <- cv_half1 <- cv_half2 <- ml_cv[, 1:3]
boundary_cv <- vector("list", 5)
for (k in 1:5) {
  test <- fold == k
  ml <- fit_ml(dat[!test, ])
  ml_cv[test, ] <- predict_ml(dat[!test, ], dat[test, ], ml)
  b <- bayes_fit(dat[!test, ], dat[test, ], seed = 5100+k)
  bayes_cv[test, ] <- bayes_summary(b)
  cv_half1[test, ] <- bayes_summary(b, 1:10000)
  cv_half2[test, ] <- bayes_summary(b, 10001:20000)
  boundary_cv[[k]] <- boundary(b)
}
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(ml_cv))),
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(bayes_cv))))
```

```{r validation-results}
comparison <- rbind(Likelihood = scores(dat$rain, ml_cv),
                    Bayesian = scores(dat$rain, bayes_cv))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 2)
ml_mean_rmse <- sqrt(mean((ml_cv$Mean-dat$rain)^2))
improvement <- comparison[1, "IS95"]-comparison[2, "IS95"]
```

The Bayesian Interval Score is **`r fmt(comparison[2, "IS95"])` mm**, compared
with **`r fmt(comparison[1, "IS95"])` mm** for likelihood kriging. This is
a decrease of **`r fmt(improvement)` mm**, or
**`r fmt(100*improvement/comparison[1, "IS95"])`%**. The result favours the
Bayesian intervals on this split, but the improvement is small.

Coverage changes from **`r fmt(comparison[1, "Coverage"])`%** to
**`r fmt(comparison[2, "Coverage"])`%**; the Bayesian intervals still do not
reach the nominal 95%. Their average width is
**`r fmt(comparison[2, "Width"])` mm**, compared with
**`r fmt(comparison[1, "Width"])` mm** for likelihood intervals.
The change in coverage corresponds to
**`r sum(dat$rain >= bayes_cv$Lower & dat$rain <= bayes_cv$Upper)-sum(dat$rain >= ml_cv$Lower & dat$rain <= ml_cv$Upper)`
additional stations** inside the intervals. This shows why coverage and
width should be read together with the score.
Median-prediction MAE differs by only
**`r fmt(abs(comparison[1, "MAE"]-comparison[2, "MAE"]))` mm**.

As a reproducibility check, the original likelihood **mean** predictions
give RMSE **`r fmt(ml_mean_rmse)` mm**, matching the revised Homework 4.
I do not compare that mean-based RMSE directly with a Bayesian median's RMSE.

```{r fold-results}
fold_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(k) {
  i <- fold == k
  data.frame(Fold = k, Stations = sum(i),
    IS95_ML = scores(dat$rain[i], ml_cv[i, ])["IS95"],
    IS95_Bayes = scores(dat$rain[i], bayes_cv[i, ])["IS95"])
}))
knitr::kable(fold_results, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The Bayesian Interval Score is lower in
**`r sum(fold_results$IS95_Bayes < fold_results$IS95_ML)` of the five folds**.
The improvement is therefore not consistent in every held-out group.
The folds share training observations, so I do
not treat these five scores as independent replicates for a significance
test. Random-fold validation mainly measures interpolation among existing
stations. It does not establish performance across a large unsampled area.

```{r prediction-check, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.6}
limits <- range(dat$rain, ml_cv$Median, bayes_cv$Median)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5))
for (method in c("Likelihood", "Bayesian")) {
  p <- if (method == "Likelihood") ml_cv else bayes_cv
  plot(dat$rain, p$Median, xlim = limits, ylim = limits, asp = 1,
       pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = "#267A8A", main = method,
       xlab = "Observed rainfall (mm)", ylab = "Held-out median (mm)")
  abline(0, 1, col = "#C45A33")
}
```

Both methods follow the broad pattern but miss some individual stations.
Their point predictions are very similar; the larger change is in the
prediction intervals.

# Parameter precision from credible intervals

```{r full-fits, cache=TRUE, cache.vars=c("full_bayes","full_ml"), cache.extra=analysis_key}
full_bayes <- bayes_fit(dat, seed = 5200, draws = 50000)
full_ml <- fit_ml(dat)
```

```{r credible-intervals}
post <- full_bayes$posterior$sample
# I calculate the nugget from each joint posterior draw.
parameter_draws <- data.frame(
  Intercept = post$beta0, Elevation = post$beta1,
  Partial_sill = post$sigmasq,
  Nugget = post$sigmasq*post$tausq.rel, Range_km = post$phi)
q <- t(vapply(parameter_draws, quantile, numeric(3),
              probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE))
credible <- data.frame(Parameter = names(parameter_draws),
  ML = c(full_ml$beta, full_ml$cov.pars[1], full_ml$nugget,
         full_ml$cov.pars[2]),
  Median = q[, 2], Lower95 = q[, 1], Upper95 = q[, 3],
  Width = q[, 3]-q[, 1])
knitr::kable(credible, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE,
  format = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "pipe")
elevation_change <- quantile(100*(exp(post$beta1/10)-1),
                            c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)
```

The elevation coefficient has a 95% credible interval above zero. In the
trend, a 100 m increase in elevation corresponds to a median increase of
about **`r fmt(elevation_change[2])`%**, with a 95% credible interval of
**`r fmt(elevation_change[1])`% to `r fmt(elevation_change[3])`%**.
This is a model-based association, not a causal effect.

The range interval is wide, so the data do not identify one distance
clearly. Range and partial sill have posterior correlation
**`r fmt(cor(post$phi, post$sigmasq))`**. I examine their joint effect below.
Partial sill and nugget are log-scale variances; their interval widths
cannot be compared directly with a range measured in km. The ML column
contains point estimates, not confidence intervals.

# What the range means for this rainfall study

Based on the feedback, I now check the correlations implied by the range,
not just whether the posterior reaches the edge of its grid.

## Geography and the prior

```{r range-geography}
pair_distance <- as.numeric(dist(dat[c("x", "y")]))
phi_values <- seq(10, 610, 20)
eta_values <- seq(0, 1.5, 0.05)
phi_prior <- exp(-phi_values/150)
phi_prior <- phi_prior/sum(phi_prior)
prior_median_phi <- phi_values[which(cumsum(phi_prior) >= 0.5)[1]]
spherical_cor <- function(h, phi) {
  u <- h/phi
  ifelse(u < 1, 1-1.5*u+0.5*u^3, 0)
}
half_fraction <- uniroot(function(u) spherical_cor(u, 1)-0.5,
                         c(0, 1))$root
```

The stations cover Basilicata and Calabria. Their north-south span is
**`r fmt(diff(range(dat$y)), 0)` km** and their east-west span is
**`r fmt(diff(range(dat$x)), 0)` km**. The greatest station separation is
**`r fmt(max(pair_distance), 0)` km**. Distances of 50, 100 and 150 km
therefore describe different parts of this regional study, rather than
only nearby stations. These distances use the coordinate units stated above.

For a spherical model, the range is where residual correlation reaches
zero. It is not a distance over which correlation stays strong. Correlation
in the spatial component falls to one-half at about **0.347 times the range**.
A range of 150 km therefore gives a half-correlation distance of about
**`r fmt(150*half_fraction, 0)` km**. Adding the nugget reduces correlation
between different stations further.

The prior puts **`r fmt(100*sum(phi_prior[phi_values > 100]), 1)`%** of its
probability above 100 km. However, its median range of
**`r prior_median_phi` km** corresponds to a half-correlation distance of only
**`r fmt(prior_median_phi*half_fraction, 0)` km** in the spatial component.
About **`r fmt(100*sum(phi_prior[phi_values > max(pair_distance)]), 1)`%**
allows ranges beyond the greatest observed separation. I treat this as an
uncertain tail of the prior, not as evidence for dependence beyond the study area.

Annual rainfall totals can share broad weather conditions. Mountains and
coastal exposure can also create differences between locations, even after
allowing for elevation. This is my reason for allowing both local and
regional dependence, while giving shorter ranges more weight. It does not
justify assuming strong correlation across the whole region. The 610 km
endpoint is a generous numerical limit, not an estimated storm size or a
known physical rainfall scale.

## Correlations at 50, 100 and 150 km

For distance $h>0$, I calculate three quantities for every posterior draw:
\[
 r(h;\phi)=\begin{cases}
 1-1.5h/\phi+0.5(h/\phi)^3,&h<\phi,\\
 0,&h\geq\phi,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad C(h)=\sigma^2 r(h;\phi),\qquad
 \rho(h)=\frac{C(h)}{\sigma^2+\tau^2}
        =\frac{r(h;\phi)}{1+\eta}.
\]
Here $r$ is the correlation of the spatial component, $C$ is its covariance,
and $\rho$ is the residual correlation between two different observations,
including the nugget. These are correlations of **log-rainfall residuals
after the elevation trend**, not correlations of raw rainfall. They describe
the residual process conditional on a parameter draw, not the full predictive
correlation after also averaging over uncertain trend coefficients.

```{r range-correlations}
summary_95 <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)
  sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", q[2], q[1], q[3])
}
distances <- c(50, 100, 150)
residual_cor <- function(h, s) spherical_cor(h, s$phi)/(1+s$tausq.rel)
range_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(distances, function(h) {
  r <- spherical_cor(h, post$phi)
  data.frame(Distance_km = h,
    Pairs_within_10km = sum(abs(pair_distance-h) <= 10),
    Correlation = summary_95(residual_cor(h, post)),
    Covariance = summary_95(post$sigmasq*r))
}))
knitr::kable(range_table, row.names = FALSE)
```

Each entry gives the posterior median and a central 95% credible interval.
Covariance is in squared log-rainfall units. Pair counts show how many
observed pairs are near each distance; pairs sharing a station are not
independent observations.

At 50 km, the median residual correlation is about **0.45**, with a 95%
interval of **0.19 to 0.75**. At 100 km it is about **0.13**, but the interval
runs from **0 to 0.56**. At 150 km the median is **zero**, while the upper
limit is about **0.39**. Thus a median range of 150 km does not mean strong
correlation at 150 km. Longer-distance dependence remains uncertain.

I keep each draw's range, partial sill and nugget together. The partial
sill cancels in the correlation formula when the nugget is expressed as
$\eta\sigma^2$, but it does not cancel in the covariance. The positive
range-sill association means that draws with longer ranges often also
have larger covariances. Multiplying separate parameter summaries would
lose this information; the covariance intervals above use the joint draws.

```{r prior-correlation-check}
prior_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(distances, function(h) {
  prior_rho <- outer(spherical_cor(h, phi_values), 1+eta_values, "/")
  data.frame(Distance_km = h,
    Prior_percent = 100*sum(phi_prior*rowMeans(prior_rho > 0.2)),
    Posterior_percent = 100*mean(residual_cor(h, post) > 0.2))
}))
knitr::kable(prior_check, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

This table gives the probability that residual correlation exceeds **0.2**.
I use 0.2 only as an easy reference, not as a scientific cutoff. In
particular, the prior probability of correlation above 0.2 at 100 km is
about **23%**, even though about half the prior range values exceed 100 km.
At 150 km the corresponding prior probability is about **11%**. This makes
the actual dependence allowed by the prior clearer than its range limits alone.

```{r residual-correlation-plot, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.8}
h <- seq(1, 350, by = 1)
corr_band <- sapply(h, function(d) {
  quantile(residual_cor(d, post), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)
})
plot(h, corr_band[2, ], type = "n", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Residual correlation")
polygon(c(h, rev(h)), c(corr_band[1, ], rev(corr_band[3, ])),
        col = "#D4E8ED", border = NA)
lines(h, corr_band[2, ], col = "#267A8A", lwd = 2)
abline(v = distances, col = "grey65", lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("Posterior median", "Pointwise 95% credible band"),
       col = c("#267A8A", "#D4E8ED"), lwd = c(2, 8), bty = "n")
```

The band describes uncertainty about residual correlation at each distance.
It is not a rainfall prediction interval or a simultaneous band. I start
above zero because independent nugget variation causes a jump between
correlation at the same observation and at two very close observations.


# Numerical checks and prior sensitivity

```{r simulation-check}
simulation_check <- rbind(
  First_10000 = scores(dat$rain, cv_half1),
  Second_10000 = scores(dat$rain, cv_half2))
knitr::kable(simulation_check, digits = 2)
edge <- apply(rbind(do.call(rbind, boundary_cv), boundary(full_bayes)), 2, max)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Boundary = names(edge),
                        Max_posterior_percent = 100*edge),
             digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)
```

The two halves of the predictive simulations give Interval Scores differing
by **`r fmt(abs(diff(simulation_check[, "IS95"])))` mm**. This is a check
on simulation noise, not on uncertainty caused by the limited station
sample. The small posterior masses at the upper grid limits suggest that
those limits are not cutting off much posterior mass. This is only a
numerical check: it does not show that the correlation scales are physically
plausible. That question is addressed by the distance-based checks above.
Zero nugget is allowed, so I report its boundary probability too.

```{r sensitivity, cache=TRUE, cache.vars=c("finer","shorter"), cache.extra=analysis_key}
finer <- bayes_fit(dat, seed = 5401, prior = make_prior(step = 10),
                   draws = 50000)
shorter <- bayes_fit(dat, seed = 5403, prior = make_prior(range_scale = 75),
                     draws = 50000)
```

```{r sensitivity-table}
sensitivity_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list(Main = full_bayes, Finer_grid = finer, Shorter_range_prior = shorter),
  function(b) {
    s <- b$posterior$sample
    slope <- quantile(s$beta1, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)
    range <- quantile(s$phi, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), names = FALSE)
    data.frame(Slope_median = slope[2],
      Slope_95 = paste(fmt(slope[1], 3), "to", fmt(slope[3], 3)),
      Range_median = range[2],
      Range_95 = paste(range[1], "to", range[3]))
  }))
knitr::kable(sensitivity_table, digits = 3)
```

The finer grid checks numerical resolution. The second prior is a more
useful check of the geographical assumption: it halves the exponential
scale from 150 to 75 km, keeping the same support and all other priors.
It gives shorter ranges more weight instead of broadening the prior again.
The 75 km scale is a sensitivity choice, not a known rainfall constant.

```{r shorter-prior-correlations}
shorter_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(distances, function(h) {
  data.frame(Distance_km = h,
    Main_prior = summary_95(residual_cor(h, post)),
    Shorter_prior = summary_95(residual_cor(h, shorter$posterior$sample)))
}))
knitr::kable(shorter_table, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE,
  format = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "pipe")
```

With the shorter-range prior, the posterior median range is **130 km**
and its 95% interval is **70 to 290 km**, compared with **150 km** and
**90 to 370 km** in the main fit. At 100 km, the median residual correlation
falls from about **0.13 to 0.06**, and its upper limit falls from **0.56 to
0.45**. The elevation estimate changes little. The long-distance part of
the model is therefore sensitive to the range prior; I do not call it robust.

I retain the original prior as a broad working choice for annual regional
rainfall. Its typical ranges imply much shorter distances of strong
correlation, and its long tail allows a possible regional component without
making it certain. I have no local evidence here that would justify ruling
out that component with a sharper prior. However, this is a modelling
judgement, not proof that every admitted scale is physically correct.
Mountains and coastal exposure may also create directional patterns that
this isotropic model misses.

The main prior and prediction model have not changed, so the validation
scores and prediction maps remain those of the main fit. The shorter prior
is a full-data interpretation check, not a second predictive comparison.
I do not claim that the scores or maps would be unchanged under it, and I
have not selected a prior using held-out rainfall.

# Prediction maps on the Homework 4 grid

For the maps I fit the model to all 189 stations. The Bayesian intervals
include uncertainty in its parameters, but not uncertainty about the
chosen transformation, trend or covariance family.

```{r grid-prediction, cache=TRUE, cache.vars=c("ml_grid","bayes_grid"), cache.extra=analysis_key}
ml_grid <- predict_ml(dat, grid, full_ml)
bayes_grid <- ml_grid[, 1:3]
# Small batches limit memory; every batch uses all 189 training stations.
groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(grid)), ceiling(seq_len(nrow(grid))/200))
for (j in seq_along(groups)) {
  i <- groups[[j]]
  b <- bayes_fit(dat, grid[i, ], seed = 5300+j, draws = 10000)
  bayes_grid[i, ] <- bayes_summary(b)
}
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(bayes_grid))),
          all(bayes_grid$Lower > 0),
          all(bayes_grid$Lower < bayes_grid$Upper))
```

Every batch uses the same full dataset and original priors. I use the
results only for pointwise summaries, not for joint probabilities across
the whole map.

```{r grid-summary}
hull <- chull(dat$x, dat$y)
outside_hull <- sp::point.in.polygon(
  grid$x, grid$y, dat$x[hull], dat$y[hull]) == 0
outside_elevation <- grid$Quota < min(dat$Quota) | grid$Quota > max(dat$Quota)
ml_width <- ml_grid$Upper-ml_grid$Lower
bayes_width <- bayes_grid$Upper-bayes_grid$Lower
map_summary <- data.frame(Method = c("Likelihood", "Bayesian"),
  Min_median = c(min(ml_grid$Median), min(bayes_grid$Median)),
  Max_median = c(max(ml_grid$Median), max(bayes_grid$Median)),
  Median_width = c(median(ml_width), median(bayes_width)))
knitr::kable(map_summary, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

The median maps have similar broad patterns. Bayesian intervals are wider
at **`r fmt(100*mean(bayes_width > ml_width), 1)`%** of grid points, but
there is no rule that a Bayesian interval must always be wider. It depends
on the data, prior and fitted covariance distribution. Differences between
the two maps are not prediction errors: grid truth is unavailable, which
is why the comparison scores come from held-out stations.

```{r map-functions}
draw_outlines <- function() {
  lines(data_env$Bas$XUTM/1000, data_env$Bas$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
  lines(data_env$Cal$XUTM/1000, data_env$Cal$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
}
draw_map <- function(values, breaks, title) {
  colours <- hcl.colors(length(breaks)-1, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE)
  plot(grid$x, grid$y, type = "n", asp = 1,
       xlim = range(c(grid$x, dat$x)), ylim = range(c(grid$y, dat$y)),
       xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)", main = title)
  points(grid$x, grid$y, pch = 15, cex = 0.55,
         col = colours[cut(values, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)])
  draw_outlines()
  points(dat$x, dat$y, pch = 20, cex = 0.18)
  points(grid$x[outside_hull], grid$y[outside_hull], pch = 4,
         cex = 0.38, col = "grey25")
  points(grid$x[outside_elevation], grid$y[outside_elevation],
         pch = 2, cex = 0.48, col = "#B33A26")
  legend("bottomleft", paste(head(breaks, -1), tail(breaks, -1), sep = " to "),
         fill = colours, title = "mm", bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
}
```

```{r comparison-maps, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=8}
median_breaks <- pretty(range(ml_grid$Median, bayes_grid$Median), n = 6)
width_breaks <- pretty(range(ml_width, bayes_width), n = 6)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.3, 0.5), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
draw_map(ml_grid$Median, median_breaks, "Likelihood predictive median")
draw_map(bayes_grid$Median, median_breaks, "Bayesian predictive median")
draw_map(ml_width, width_breaks, "Likelihood 95% interval width")
draw_map(bayes_width, width_breaks, "Bayesian 95% interval width")
```

The two median maps share a scale, and the two width maps share another.
Black dots are stations, crosses mark the **`r sum(outside_hull)` points
outside their convex hull**, and red triangles mark the
**`r sum(outside_elevation)` points outside the observed elevation range**.
The groups may overlap. The supplied grid reaches 1,995 m, while the
highest observed station is 1,369 m. Bayesian inference does not remove
the need to be cautious about those extrapolated predictions.

```{r bayesian-limits, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.2}
limit_breaks <- pretty(range(bayes_grid$Lower, bayes_grid$Upper), n = 6)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5))
draw_map(bayes_grid$Lower, limit_breaks, "Lower 95% predictive limit")
draw_map(bayes_grid$Upper, limit_breaks, "Upper 95% predictive limit")
```

These are **posterior predictive limits for rainfall**, not credible
intervals for a parameter. The log transformation keeps them positive.
Wider intervals in wet areas partly reflect the back-transformation:
the same uncertainty on the log scale gives a larger width in mm at a
higher rainfall level. Width is therefore not a map of station density alone.

# What I would take from the comparison

For 1970, the Bayesian fit gives a similar rainfall pattern to Homework 4,
with a modest improvement in the held-out Interval Score. The point
predictions are very similar, and the coverage improvement is small.
I would not claim that one successful split proves general superiority.

The elevation effect is positive, but the range is less certain. The new
checks show moderate residual correlation at 50 km and weaker, less certain
correlation at 100 and 150 km. The shorter-range prior reduces the evidence
for long-distance dependence. I retain the broad prior as a working choice,
while making this sensitivity clear.

The comparison uses one random split and the model selected in Homework 4.
The results still depend on the priors and on the Gaussian, stationary and
isotropic residual model. The Bayesian intervals include parameter
uncertainty, but their observed coverage is still below 95%.

# Sources and software

I used the revised Homework 4 model and the supplied course notes
*Chapter6-11*, especially the distinction between parameter and predictive
uncertainty and the Interval Score in Section 10.3. I also checked the
`geoR` documentation and implementation of `krige.bayes`, `prior.control`,
`model.control`, `output.control` and the spherical correlation in
`cov.spatial`. In particular, the priors use a
relative nugget, the trend has a flat prior, and the observation target
requires `signal = FALSE`.

```{r versions}
packages <- c("geoR", "sp", "knitr", "rmarkdown")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Component = c("R", packages),
  Version = c(as.character(getRversion()),
    vapply(packages, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)),
           character(1)))), row.names = FALSE)
```
